report:
**Conclusion: probably no—not reliably.** Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) is biologically plausible because statins affect the pathway that produces CoQ10, but this does not prove that low CoQ10 causes statin muscle symptoms or that supplements correct them.

The clinical evidence is conflicting and limited. A 2018 meta-analysis of randomized trials reported lower scores for pain, weakness, cramps and tiredness with CoQ10, but the trials were generally small, short, and used differing symptom definitions and doses—features that make the pooled result uncertain.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30371340/

Conversely, a later systematic review/meta-analysis found no statistically significant improvement in statin-related muscle pain or in ability to remain adherent to statin therapy. Reviews of the topic characterize the evidence as inconsistent and insufficient for a routine recommendation.  
https://www.endocrinologyadvisor.com/news/coq10-therapy-may-not-improve-statin-adherence-or-relieve-associated-muscle-pain-in-statin-associated-myalgia/  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9171566/

A more recent double-blind placebo-controlled trial also investigated whether CoQ10 changes muscle CoQ10/mitochondrial measures in statin-treated people, reflecting that the proposed mechanism remains unresolved rather than established.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36139772/

So, your “yes” is possible for an individual, but current evidence does **not** show dependable symptom relief. Do not stop a statin because of muscle discomfort without speaking to the prescriber: assessing other causes, temporarily stopping/rechallenging, changing dose or statin, or using non-statin lipid-lowering treatment has stronger clinical support.
